o: Repeatedly remove each row's maximum; each round, add the largest of those maxima to the score. Sorting every row once reveals that round r's candidates are simply column r (0-indexed from the right) of the sorted rows — so the score is Σ over columns of the column maximum. Example 1: sorted rows give column maxima 7, 5, 3 → 15.
k: Sorting rows turns 'remove the max' into 'consume columns left to right'.
Score = Σ_c max over rows of sortedRow[c].

a.n: Approach 1: Sort rows, take column maxima
a.i: After sorting each row ascending, the k-th removal from that row is its k-th largest, i.e., sortedRow[len−1−k]. The best among rows in round k is therefore the max of that column. Sum these maxima.
s: For each column index c, add max over rows of row[c].
a.t: O(R·C log C) — sorting each of R rows of length C dominates

a.i: Directly simulate the process: heapify each row (as a max-heap), and for C rounds pop one element per row, adding the round's maximum to the score. This mirrors the statement verbatim and is useful when rows arrive as streams.
s: Heapify each row (negate values for Python/JS min-heaps).
For each of C rounds: peek/pop one element per row; add the largest to the score.
a.t: O(R·C log C) — heapify plus C rounds of pops

w: Prefer the sort-and-column-max version for brevity. Pitfall: rows may have different lengths per constraints?
